titre: The Noise They Couldn't Silence Was the Echo of the Big Bang
accroche: An antenna picks up a constant noise, from every direction, that no cleaning makes go away. Another team was about to look for it.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1964, at Crawford Hill, New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson test a horn antenna built five years earlier for NASA's Echo communications satellite project. To measure very faint signals, they first have to eliminate every recognizable source of interference from their receiver.

## An excess of noise that nothing explains

Their instrument picks up an excess antenna temperature that they cannot explain: at a frequency of 4,080 megahertz, it measures about 3.5 kelvins more than expected, once 2.3 kelvins are counted for sky absorption and 0.9 for the instrument. The signal is the same day and night, and whichever direction of the sky is observed: isotropic, and unpolarized.

Suspecting a hardware flaw, the two researchers take the antenna apart piece by piece. Pigeons had nested in the antenna; they remove them, and clean out the accumulated droppings. The noise does not change. Nothing explains the excess.

## One team was looking for it, the other found it without looking

What they do not know is that, in the same state, at Princeton University, Robert Dicke's team (with James Peebles, Peter Roll and David Wilkinson) is preparing a receiver to look for precisely this signal: a leftover radiation that, according to their theoretical calculations, should fill the whole universe if it was born in a hot, dense state. A friend of Penzias, the physicist Bernard Burke, tells him about a paper by Peebles on such a radiation; Penzias calls Dicke, and the link is made: the noise Penzias and Wilson could not silence is the radiation the Princeton team was about to search for, without yet having a result.

The two teams publish side by side, in the same July 1965 issue of the Astrophysical Journal: the observation, signed by Penzias and Wilson, and its cosmological interpretation, signed by Dicke's group. Penzias and Wilson will receive the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978 for their detection; Peebles will receive his in 2019 for his theoretical work in cosmology. They had found without looking what another team, at the same moment and in the same state, was about to look for methodically.

The lesson usually drawn from this, that chance rewards prepared minds, leaves out half the story: here, two distinct preparations, one theoretical and the other instrumental, had to meet, through an intermediary and then a phone call, for the discovery to be recognized for what it was.

repere.texte: The Holmdel antenna measured, at 4,080 megahertz, an antenna temperature about 3.5 kelvins higher than expected, isotropic and unpolarized.
repere.source: Penzias, A. A. & Wilson, R. W., “A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s,” The Astrophysical Journal, 142, 419-421, 1965

carte.punch: The noise they couldn't silence was the echo of the Big Bang
carte.idee: In 1964, two Bell Labs researchers measure a constant radio noise, coming from every direction, that cleaning the antenna does not make go away. In the same state, a Princeton team was about to search for this very signal, predicted by Big Bang theory.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Penzias & Wilson, “A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s,” full text (ADS)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The first page of the paper: an excess of about 3.5 K, isotropic and unpolarized.

quiz.question: Why was the phone call between Bell Labs and Princeton decisive?
choix: Because Princeton's team had a more sensitive instrument, which Penzias and Wilson then borrowed
Because it linked an unexplained observation to a theoretical prediction that the other side was just about to try to verify
Because the two teams had actually been working on the same project from the start
Because it revealed that the measured noise actually came from the pigeons, not from cosmic radiation
quiz.explication: Dicke's team had predicted this leftover radiation and was preparing a receiver to search for it, without yet having a result; Penzias and Wilson had the instrument and the signal, but not the theory. The two teams remained separate, and cleaning out the pigeons had not made the noise go away.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Penzias and Wilson do when they suspected a hardware flaw in their antenna?
choix: They waited six months to see whether the signal varied with the seasons
They took the antenna apart piece by piece, removed pigeons, and cleaned out the accumulated droppings
They replaced the whole antenna with a newer model
They sent the receiver to Princeton's team for verification
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Suspecting a hardware flaw, Penzias and Wilson take the antenna apart piece by piece; they remove pigeons that had nested in it and clean out the accumulated droppings, but the noise does not change.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What project was the Holmdel antenna built for, five years before the 1964 measurements?
choix: Listening for possible extraterrestrial radio signals
A radar program for the United States Army
Robert Dicke's team at Princeton University
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Crawford Hill horn antenna had been built in 1959, five years before the 1964 measurements, for NASA's Echo communications satellite project, not to search for cosmic radiation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was the link made between Penzias and Wilson's observation and Dicke's team's theory?
choix: A national newspaper announced the discovery before the two teams met
Dicke read Penzias and Wilson's paper in the Astrophysical Journal before contacting them
Bernard Burke, a friend of Penzias, told him about a paper by Peebles, and Penzias called Dicke
The two teams shared the same lab director at Bell Labs
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bernard Burke, a friend of Penzias, tells him about a paper by Peebles on this predicted radiation; Penzias then calls Dicke, linking the unexplained observation to the theory Princeton was about to verify.
